title: Seventy Days South
story:
It was the seventieth morning since James had first set foot outside the Great Canopy. Seventy days of learning that the earth did not end where the green branches parted, but simply kept unrolling in stone, river, and sky. The lush jungle leaves that once sheltered him felt a lifetime away; the high clockworks of Oakhaven seemed like an echo from another world; even Don Tadeo's sweet-scented cedar shavings were now several days behind him on the northern trail.

He walked through tall amber grass that rasped softly against his knees. He walked past towering agaves whose withered flower spikes stood like weathered spears against the pale sky. He walked beneath the steady arc of the morning sun, his brass compass cool against his chest, its needle swaying slightly with every step before settling stubbornly south. In the dry highland heat, the world was quiet in a way he had never known—not the hushed, damp silence of the canopy, but an open, breathless stillness carried on a dry wind.

By midday, the limestone arch of yesterday was lost among the rolling ridges behind him. The trail dwindled into a faint cart track rutted into pale dirt, bordered by crumbled fieldstones where terraced plots had long been surrendered to thistle and dust. Pausing under the meager shade of a solitary twisted acacia, James unstopped his water and smoothed out Barnaby’s map. His own charcoal line now stretched well past the paper’s edge, wandering into the white margin of things yet to be named. There was a strange comfort in that blank space, an invitation written in empty paper.

As the afternoon cooled into a hazy ochre, the trail crested a barren ridge of pale chalk. Below lay a desolate, shadowy hollow where the scrub gave way to scattered, unkempt pastures and a distant, sprawling cluster of weathered roofs. No bright kites danced above those chimneys; no sound of church bells or cheerful market calls drifted up the slope. A sudden gust of wind whipped over the ridge, carrying a faint, acrid smell of coal smoke and dry dust. James tucked the compass into his fur, tightened the colorful woven strap across his shoulder, and watched the grey settlement sit silently in the deepening dusk.
